canonical_statement: The review aimed to indirectly compare licensed SGLT-2 inhibitors for glycaemic, weight and systolic blood-pressure efficacy in adults with type 2 diabetes and to examine whether canagliflozin might be more potent than other agents.
The monotherapy evidence base comprised adults with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled with diet and exercise alone.

canonical_statement: The dual-therapy evidence base comprised adults with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on metformin monotherapy.

canonical_statement: Eligible studies were randomized controlled trials of licensed SGLT-2 inhibitor doses with a minimum treatment duration of 24 weeks.

canonical_statement: Eligible trials had to report the proportion achieving HbA1c <7% and/or mean HbA1c change; weight and systolic blood pressure were additionally sought.

canonical_statement: MEDLINE, MEDLINE In-Process and EMBASE were searched from January 2005 through September 2014, with an update in January 2015.
Study selection, data extraction and risk-of-bias assessment were performed by one reviewer and checked by a second reviewer.
Risk of bias was assessed with the Cochrane tool across sequence generation, allocation concealment, outcome-assessor blinding, incomplete outcome data and selective reporting.
The dichotomous glycaemic outcome was achievement of HbA1c <7.0%.

outcome.definition: Proportion of participants achieving HbA1c below 7.0% at approximately 24–26 weeks

canonical_statement: A continuous glycaemic outcome was mean change in HbA1c from baseline.

canonical_statement: A secondary efficacy outcome was mean change in body weight from baseline.

canonical_statement: The Bayesian network meta-analysis was implemented in WinBUGS 1.4.3, preserved within-trial randomization and accounted for correlations in multi-arm trials.
Model convergence was assessed using trace plots and Brooks–Gelman–Rubin statistics with two chains; 20,000 samples were discarded and results were based on a further 70,000 samples.
A fixed-effect network meta-analysis was used based on deviance information criterion and the small number of studies contributing to comparisons.
Direct and indirect evidence were compared for inconsistency when a single common comparator allowed the comparison.
The prespecified sensitivity strategy included atypical trials by Bolinder, Henry and Kashiwagi to evaluate the stability of dual-therapy estimates.
DigitizeIt was used to derive an SD from a published figure when one canagliflozin study did not provide the needed numeric SD.

The supplementary Ovid MEDLINE strategy combined randomized-trial/systematic-review terms, type 2 diabetes terms and named SGLT-2 inhibitor/SGLT-2 terms, then limited results to English-language human studies from 2005 onward.

The search retrieved 535 abstracts; 73 duplicates were removed, 462 records were screened by title/abstract, 417 were excluded, 45 full texts were assessed, and the article states that 13 trials met inclusion criteria.

The article states that 13 trials were included, but its drug-specific counts enumerate 6 dapagliflozin, 3 canagliflozin, 2 empagliflozin, and one each of luseogliflozin, ipragliflozin and tofogliflozin trials, which sums to 14; this is an internal source-count inconsistency.
Eight trials contributed monotherapy comparisons with placebo and six trials contributed dual-therapy comparisons on a metformin background.
Most included trials were judged high quality with low risk of bias, although several domains were unclear because reporting was insufficient.
All included trials were funded by pharmaceutical companies.

In monotherapy, every SGLT-2 inhibitor was significantly more effective than placebo for HbA1c target attainment, HbA1c reduction and weight reduction; all reduced systolic blood pressure, but dapagliflozin 10 mg and tofogliflozin 10 and 40 mg did not reach statistical significance for SBP because of wide intervals.

The authors concluded that there were few clinically significant efficacy differences among SGLT-2 inhibitors; in monotherapy HbA1c reductions were largest with canagliflozin and smallest with dapagliflozin, while HbA1c differences were insignificant in dual therapy.
The authors interpreted the absence of a consistent canagliflozin advantage in dual therapy as suggesting that its additional SGLT-1 activity may not be clinically significant.
The main limitation was the lack of head-to-head randomized trials; the network therefore relied heavily on indirect comparisons.
Only a small number of trials contributed evidence to several network comparisons, leading to imprecision and wide credible intervals.

Canagliflozin 300 mg was randomized directly in trials, whereas usual clinical use would begin at 100 mg and titrate only if response were insufficient, limiting direct practice translation of the 300-mg ranking.
Trial populations differed materially in baseline BMI, with Chinese and Japanese studies around 25–26 kg/m² and European studies around 28 to nearly 34 kg/m².
Incomplete outcome reporting prevented all drugs and studies from contributing to every network outcome.
The review treated 26-week canagliflozin outcomes as comparable with 24-week outcomes for other agents.
The review did not compare safety outcomes across SGLT-2 inhibitors.
Included randomized trials lasted no more than approximately 26 weeks, so long-term efficacy and adverse effects were not established.
The review itself received no specific grant from public, commercial or not-for-profit funding agencies.
Deepson Shyangdan had joined Eli Lilly by publication but was employed by the University of Warwick when the review was undertaken.
The authors disclosed involvement in NICE technology appraisals of empagliflozin, dapagliflozin and the class monotherapy appraisal.
The article states that no additional data are available.
